### Legal Issue
[Identify the core legal problem or question presented by the user.]
A municipal authority has repeatedly failed to collect garbage, leading to accumulated waste, foul smell, sanitation problems, and grave or widespread danger to public health, while the user has preserved various proofs of complaints and media.

### Applicable Law
[Identify the relevant law, statute, or constitutional provision that applies, e.g., "Sale of Goods Act, 1930 — Section X".]
Supreme Court of India jurisprudence regarding the statutory duty of authorities to maintain public order, prevent danger to public health, and address activities causing grave or widespread danger to life, property, or public health [7].

### Legal Position
[Synthesize the legal position based on the retrieved provisions. Explain what the law establishes.]
The retrieved text establishes that activities causing or likely to cause harm, danger, alarm, a feeling of insecurity among the general public, or a grave/widespread danger to life, property, or public health adversely affect public order [7]. Designated authorities—such as District Magistrates and Commissioners of Police—have a statutory duty to maintain public order and deal swiftly with situations where public order or public health is affected or apprehended to be affected by dangerous or anti-social activities/conditions [7].

### Application to Facts
[Explain how those provisions relate to the user's specific scenario.]
The accumulation of garbage over several weeks causing foul smell and serious sanitation problems constitutes a grave or widespread danger to public health [7]. While the user has approached the municipal helpline and local ward office, the established legal framework recognizes that situations affecting public health require swift and effective action by authorities having a statutory duty to protect the public [7].

### Evidence / Reasoning
[Provide concise reasoning linking the facts to the law, citing specific evidence from the retrieved text, e.g., "Section X provides that..."]
The reasoning is derived from the principle that actions or conditions resulting in a grave or widespread danger to public health adversely affect the public order and community well-being [7]. The state and local authorities are recognized as having the satisfaction and duty to curb conditions that cause harm or danger to public health, allowing designated officers to move swiftly where public health is affected [7]. The user's collected evidence (photographs, videos, complaint numbers, dates, and communications) serves to substantiate the existence of this public health hazard and the administrative inaction.

### Remedies / Next Steps
[Only provide remedies supported by the retrieved sources. If none, state what is missing or that the retrieved provisions do not establish a specific remedy for the facts provided.]
The retrieved sources establish that designated authorities (such as District Magistrates and Commissioners of Police) have a statutory duty to move swiftly when public health or public order is affected [7]. However, the specific civil remedies, writ procedures, or statutory municipal grievance sections are not contained in the provided text. Therefore, the retrieved text does not detail an exact step-by-step municipal escalation hierarchy or court remedy outside of identifying that authorities have a statutory duty to deal with conditions causing danger to public health.

### Relevant Authorities
[List the citations in a meaningful way, e.g., "[1] Sale of Goods Act, 1930 — Section X -> Read relevant provision"]
- [7] Supreme Court of India, None v. None — Regarding statutory duties of authorities to swiftly address conditions causing harm, danger, or grave/widespread danger to public health and public order.

activities of various persons mentioned in the preamble with

power conferred by sub-s. (1) of sec.3. It is seen that  the
dangerous  or  anti  social  activities  are   legislatively
recognised  to be prejudicial to the maintenance  of  public
order.   The enumerated activities hereinbefore referred  to
are  not  isolated but being indulged in from time  to  time
adversely  affecting the public order and even  tempo.   The
Dist.    Magistrate  concerned,  being  the  highest   Dist.
Officer  on the spot and the Commissioner of Police  in  the
cities  have  statutory  duty  to  maintain  public   order.

Govt. having exercised the power under s. 3 (2) conferred on
the Dist.  Magistrate or the Commissioner the power to order
detention under s.3(1) when he considers or deems  necessary
to  detain  any person involved in any of the  dangerous  or
anti    social    activities    enumerated     hereinbefore,
